data.title: House Robber
data.summary:
Input: An array of non-negative integers representing money stashed in each house.
Output: The maximum amount of money you can rob tonight without alerting the police by robbing two adjacent houses.
Rules: You cannot rob two adjacent houses.

data.key_insight: For each house, we have two choices: either rob it (adding its money to the maximum amount from two houses ago) or skip it (keeping the maximum amount from the previous house).

steps.title: Handle Base Cases
steps.detail: If the input list is empty, return 0. If there is only one house, return its value.

steps.title: Initialize DP State
steps.detail: Keep track of the maximum money robbed up to the house two steps back (prev2) and one step back (prev1).

steps.title: Iterate Through Houses
steps.detail: For each house from index 2 onwards, compute the current maximum as max(prev1, prev2 + current_house_money), then update prev2 and prev1 accordingly.

steps.title: Return Result
steps.detail: After checking all houses, prev1 holds the maximum money that can be robbed.

data.pattern_summary: Dynamic Programming breaks a problem down into overlapping subproblems, storing the results of previous decisions to build up the optimal solution for larger inputs.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic Programming
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. Each house choice depends on the optimal results of the previous houses, allowing us to build up the answer efficiently.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers usually work on sorted arrays or sliding windows, but here we need to evaluate non-contiguous combinations and overlapping subproblems.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Taking the local maximum at each house will prevent you from getting the global maximum because you cannot pick adjacent houses.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. A hash map helps with O(1) lookups of frequencies or values, but it does not solve sequential decision-making constraints.

signals.hint: Signals an optimization problem where we want to find the absolute best outcome among many possibilities.

signals.phrase: without alerting the police by robbing two adjacent houses
signals.hint: Introduces a restriction on the choices you can make, linking your current decision directly to your previous decision.

data.brute_force_idea: Generate every possible combination of houses to rob, filter out any combination that includes adjacent houses, and find the maximum sum among the valid combinations.
data.brute_force_why: There are 2^n possible subsets of houses, and for each subset, checking validity and summing takes additional time.
data.bottleneck: Iterating through all subsets using itertools.combinations generates an exponential number of choices, many of which share overlapping subproblems.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many subsets are generated as the number of houses grows.
Notice how checking combinations recalculates sums for overlapping house selections repeatedly.
Ask yourself if you really need to test every single subset from scratch, or if knowing the best answer for the first k houses helps you find the answer for k+1 houses.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach recomputes combinations of valid house selections, resulting in exponential time. The optimized dynamic programming approach removes this bottleneck by keeping track of only the maximum money possible up to the previous two houses, reducing the decision at each step to a single constant-time comparison.

derivation.note: The loop runs linearly from index 2 to the end of the input array.
Calculates the maximum between skipping or robbing the current house using simple arithmetic and comparisons.
Shifts the window forward by assigning prev1 to prev2.
Updates prev1 with the newly calculated current max.

data.time_summary: Lines 11 through 14 execute a constant number of operations inside a single loop of size n - 2. As n grows, the step count scales linearly with the input size, yielding O(n) time complexity.
data.space_summary: Only a fixed set of scalar variables (prev2, prev1, current) are used to store intermediate states, requiring no extra data structures that scale with input size. This yields O(1) space complexity.
data.takeaway: When a problem asks for an optimal sequence where adjacent elements cannot be chosen, look for overlapping subproblems and maintain only the rolling state of the previous decisions rather than generating all combinations.
mistakes: Failing to handle edge cases where the input array has length less than 2, leading to index errors.
Using an array to store all past DP states when only the last two values are needed for the calculation.
Confusing the decision to rob the current house by incorrectly adding it to prev1 instead of prev2.

events.label: Tutor: build the visual explanation

data.overview: The House Robber problem calculates the maximum money you can rob from a row of houses without robbing two adjacent ones. It uses dynamic programming to keep track of the optimal amount at each step by comparing choices of robbing or skipping.
data.intuition: Imagine walking down a street of houses where alarms trigger if you rob neighbors. At each house, you look back: your best total is either skipping this house (keeping the last house's total) or robbing this house (adding its loot to the total from two houses ago).
